territorial_scope.description: Applies to data brokers under the California Civil Code provisions it adds and amends, which define covered businesses by their collection and sale of consumers' personal information.

evidence.quote: “Data broker” means a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer with whom the business does not have a direct relationship.

agora_harms: Violation of civil or human rights, including privacy

summary.short: Requires data brokers to register with the California Privacy Protection Agency and honor consumer deletion requests through an accessible deletion mechanism the agency must establish by January 1, 2026; broker deletion duties apply from August 1, 2026, with triennial audits from 2028 and administrative fines.
summary.long: Amends Civil Code Sections 1798.99.80 to 1798.99.89 on data brokers, defined as businesses that knowingly sell to third parties personal information of consumers with whom they have no direct relationship. Data brokers must register with the California Privacy Protection Agency by January 31 each year, pay a fee, and disclose specified information, including whether they collect minors' data, precise geolocation or reproductive health care data. The agency must establish by January 1, 2026 an accessible deletion mechanism through which a consumer can, with one verifiable request, ask all registered brokers to delete their personal information. From August 1, 2026, brokers must access the mechanism at least every 45 days, delete the consumer's data within 45 days, and not sell or share new personal information of requesting consumers. Brokers must undergo an independent audit every three years from January 1, 2028. Failure to register carries fines of $200 per day; failure to comply with deletion duties carries $200 per deletion request per day, plus fees and agency costs. Penalties and fees go to the Data Brokers' Registry Fund, administered by the agency.

relations.note: Amends four existing Civil Code sections and adds four new sections (Secs. 1–8 of the act).

notes: Text is the chaptered version of SB 362 (Chapter 709, Statutes of 2023, chaptered 2023-10-10) as supplied; later amendments are not in the document. Businesses and data brokers are addressees but no named firms appear, so no firm entities are recorded. Internal points: (1) § 1798.99.86(f)(1) sets an access fee for accessing the mechanism 'pursuant to subdivision (d)', but the access duty appears in subdivision (c)(1); subdivision (d) concerns sales and sharing after deletion. (2) § 1798.99.82(c) and (d) impose fines in an 'administrative action', while § 1798.99.82(c)(3) refers to expenses 'as the court deems appropriate'. (3) Registration disclosure of audit status starts January 1, 2029 (§ 1798.99.82(b)(2)(F)), while the audit duty starts January 1, 2028 (§ 1798.99.86(e)(1)). The digest refers to the Attorney General as the former registration authority; that is not in the enacted operative text.
